# Thermochemistry — chapter overview blocks

::: overview ch02
answers: How does heat flow during chemical and physical changes, and how much thermal energy is stored in matter? [p.6: "This chapter applies those ideas to the heat that flows during chemical and physical changes, and to the thermal energy stored in matter."]
big-picture: It builds on Chapter 1: energy is the capacity to supply heat or do work, and the joule is its SI unit. [p.6: "In Chapter 1 you learned that energy is the capacity to supply heat or do work, and that the joule is the SI unit of energy."]
:::

::: must-know ch02
point: Heat is thermal energy moving between bodies at different temperatures; temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles. [p.13: "Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between bodies at different temperatures, and temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles."] (covers: SUM-ch02-1)
point: Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body. [p.6: "Heat always flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body"]
point: Endothermic processes absorb heat, so the surroundings get colder; exothermic processes release heat, so the surroundings get warmer. [p.13: "Endothermic processes absorb heat; exothermic processes release heat."] [p.7: "so the surroundings become colder"] [p.7: "so the surroundings become warmer"] (covers: SUM-ch02-2)
point: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C, and it does not depend on the amount. [p.13: "The specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g by 1 °C."] [p.8: "it depends only on the kind of substance, not on the amount"] (covers: SUM-ch02-3)
point: q = m × c × ΔT gives the heat for a temperature change without a phase change, with ΔT as final minus initial temperature. [p.13: "The heat for a temperature change is q = m × c × ΔT."] [p.8: "changes temperature without changing phase"] [p.8: "final temperature minus initial temperature"] (covers: SUM-ch02-4)
point: Calorimeters measure heat flow; in a coffee-cup calorimeter the water's temperature change gives the heat. [p.13: "Calorimeters measure heat flow."] [p.9: "the temperature change of the water is used to calculate the heat released or absorbed by the reaction"] (covers: SUM-ch02-5)
point: Enthalpy is H = U + PV, and it is a state function. [p.13: "Enthalpy is H = U + PV."] [p.11: "enthalpy is a state function"] (covers: SUM-ch02-6)
point: At constant pressure ΔH equals the heat absorbed or released: positive for endothermic processes, negative for exothermic ones. [p.13: "At constant pressure, the enthalpy change equals the heat absorbed or released."] [p.13: "ΔH is positive for endothermic processes and negative for exothermic processes."] (covers: SUM-ch02-7, SUM-ch02-8)
:::

::: map ch02
link: T-heat -> T-temperature | heat flows between bodies at different temperatures [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
link: T-system -> T-surroundings | the surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it [p.7: "The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it."]
link: T-endothermic-process -> T-surroundings | an endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings"]
link: T-exothermic-process -> T-surroundings | an exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings [p.7: "An exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings"]
link: T-specific-heat-capacity -> EQ-2.1 | c in the formula is the specific heat [p.8: "c is the specific heat in J/(g·°C)"]
link: T-calorimeter -> EQ-2.1 | the water's temperature change is used to calculate the heat [p.9: "the temperature change of the water is used to calculate the heat released or absorbed by the reaction"]
link: T-enthalpy -> EQ-2.2 | enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume [p.11: "equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume"]
link: T-enthalpy-change -> EQ-2.3 | at constant pressure the enthalpy change equals the heat absorbed or released [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"]
:::

::: compare CMP-ch02-01
items: T-endothermic-process | T-exothermic-process
row: Heat flow | absorbs heat from the surroundings [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings"] | releases heat to the surroundings [p.7: "An exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings"]
row: Surroundings become | colder [p.7: "absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder"] | warmer [p.7: "releases heat to the surroundings, so the surroundings become warmer"]
row: Sign of ΔH | positive [p.11: "For an endothermic reaction, the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive."] | negative [p.11: "For an exothermic reaction, the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative."]
row: Example | melting ice [p.7: "Melting ice is endothermic."] | burning wood [p.7: "Burning wood is exothermic."]
:::

::: compare CMP-ch02-02
items: T-heat | T-enthalpy
row: What it is | a transfer of thermal energy between bodies at different temperatures [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."] | a property of a system: internal energy plus pressure times volume [p.11: "Enthalpy (H) is a property of a system equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume"]
row: Depends on the path? | yes, heat depends on the path taken [p.11: "Unlike heat, which depends on the path taken"] | no, enthalpy is a state function [p.11: "enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states of the system."]
:::

::: compare CMP-ch02-03
items: T-system | T-surroundings
row: What it is | the specific portion of matter being studied [p.7: "The system is the specific portion of matter being studied"] | everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it [p.7: "The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it."]
row: In an endothermic process | heat flows into it [p.7: "In an endothermic process, heat flows into the system from the surroundings."] | it loses heat and becomes colder [p.7: "absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder"]
:::

::: compare CMP-ch02-04
items: T-temperature | T-heat
row: What it is | a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles [p.6: "Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of matter."] | the transfer of thermal energy between bodies at different temperatures [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
row: Depends on the amount of matter? | no [p.6: "Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter present"] | yes, the amount transferred does [p.6: "whereas the amount of heat transferred does"]
:::

::: strategy ch02
row: A mass and a temperature change are given and you need the heat | use q = m × c × ΔT with ΔT = final minus initial [p.8: "ΔT is the change in temperature (final temperature minus initial temperature)"]
row: You must classify a reaction from ΔH | positive ΔH means endothermic, negative ΔH means exothermic [p.13: "ΔH is positive for endothermic processes and negative for exothermic processes."]
row: A coffee-cup calorimeter problem | assume the heat released by the reaction equals the heat absorbed by the water [p.10: "we assume that the heat released by the reaction equals the heat absorbed by the water"]
:::
